title: Thoughts on behaviour
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino, a former scientist who moved into teaching, tells the story of how she learned to manage behaviour. She recounts a first school visit in which a student sprayed deodorant in her face, then a run of early-career lessons with disruption, swearing, unsafe practicals and students leaving through the wrong door, behaviour that left her going home to cry. Her turning point came when she realised the biggest difference she could make was introducing good routines, replacing novelty starters and games with a short quiz, mini-whiteboards and consistent behaviour management. Reading Tom Bennett's Running the Room persuaded her that behaviour has to be explicitly taught, and Adam Boxer's blog helped her classroom change. She concludes that clear routines and expectations, set within a wider school culture, are a way of showing students that all of them can participate and learn. It is a candid personal narrative about classroom management and teacher resilience.
points: Early-career disruption is common and can drive talented new teachers close to quitting, so the account is useful reassurance.
Varied, game-like starters were a weaker foundation than a predictable routine such as a short quiz at the start of every lesson.
Behaviour is something to be explicitly taught, an idea she took from Tom Bennett's Running the Room.
Consistency in behaviour management and clear expectations made her students listen more, feel belonging and become more confident.
Classroom structures work best as part of a wider school culture, and they signal that the teacher cares that all students can learn.
quotes: I reacted quickly by shutting my eyes and my glasses helped too but I was in shock. So much so that I didn’t report it. And because the rest of the class was unsettled and noisy, nobody noticed.

Whilst training and in the early years of my new career, I taught classes where students disrupted lessons, swore, didn’t follow instructions especially during practicals, with a student once singeing their eyebrows in a disastrous practical lesson. I had students mock my accent and parents complain about detentions I had given out.

I also taught several students who did listen and who were polite, kind, respectful and truly wonderful to teach. And I really enjoyed teaching my subject and improving my explanations. But poor behaviour was making me go home and cry.

As I gained in experience, confidence and read widely to improve my teaching, I realised that the biggest difference I could make in the classroom was to introduce good routines. Before that, I would start my lessons with an engaging starter that was completely different in structure and content each lesson or create games to help students focus or plan market-place activities.

So I changed the starts of my lessons to begin with a short quiz, started using mini-whiteboards more and became more consistent with my behaviour management. I read Running the Room by Tom Bennett and was struck by how he described behaviour as something we need to explicitly teach our students.
When we have good structures in the classroom and throughout school, it shows we care. We care that all students can participate and that all students can learn.
